preamble: You want to see everything a company makes, and the obvious place to look is the navigation bar. But a nav menu is never a full list — it's a shortlist, a handful of popular items chosen to keep the menu short. So this task has two halves: find the menu that's about products at all, then find the small door at the bottom of it that leads to the real, complete index.
generalization: Navigation menus are edited for length, not completeness. When a menu drops open and shows you six things, assume six is a design decision rather than the truth — and look at the last entry, because that's where sites habitually park the link to the full set. 'More', 'See all', 'View all', 'A–Z': different words, same door.

steps.intent: Everything on this site is organised around what it sells, so there's a top-level menu devoted to that. Opening it costs nothing and tells you immediately whether the site thinks of its products as a browsable catalogue or something you're expected to search for by name.
hints: You don't know any product names yet, so searching won't help. You want the menu that's about the things themselves.
In the navigation strip across the top of the page, in the header.

steps.intent: Six items opened up, and that's the shortlist — the ones the site wants to push, not the ones it sells. The entry at the end of a menu like this is the site admitting the menu is incomplete. Follow it and you land on the page that has to be exhaustive, because it's the only one that isn't competing for space.
hints: Count what appeared. Does a company like this really make exactly six things? One of these entries isn't a product at all.
The last entry in the menu that just dropped open, set apart from the named items above it.
